system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2162-01-19 13:45:00 to 2162-01-21 15:39:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 1 diabetes, poorly controlled with prior DKA admissions, alcohol use disorder in recovery, and depression presented with nausea, vomiting, and hyperglycemia. She was diagnosed with diabetic ketoacidosis likely triggered by a urinary tract infection. She was treated in the emergency department with IV fluids, an insulin drip, and ceftriaxone. After stabilization, she was admitted to the medicine service, transitioned back to her home insulin regimen, and completed a short course of oral antibiotics. Her condition improved rapidly, with resolution of DKA and stable vital signs. She was discharged home with instructions to continue insulin, complete antibiotics, and follow up with her primary care provider and specialists within one week.
problems: Type 1 diabetes mellitus with ketoacidosis without coma
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Type 1 diabetes mellitus with diabetic neuropathy, unspecified
Long term (current) use of insulin
Alcohol abuse, uncomplicated
Type 1 diabetes mellitus with unspecified diabetic retinopathy without macular edema
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Essential (primary) hypertension
Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery without angina pectoris
Personal history of nicotine dependence

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been really sick—nauseous all day, throwing up, and I’ve had diarrhea. My stomach hurts too, kind of crampy and all over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you had a fever, cough, or any pain when you urinate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or cough. And I haven’t noticed anything strange with my urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I see you have type 1 diabetes. Have you been checking your blood sugar lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s the thing—I haven’t been able to. My glucometer broke, and I couldn’t get a new one. So I’ve been taking my long-acting insulin, but not the fast-acting one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your blood sugar came back very high—706—and your labs show you’re in diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. That’s why you’re feeling so sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I’ve been here before for that. Is it bad this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we’re treating it. You’re getting fluids through your IV and an insulin drip to bring your levels down. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. I also had a couple of heavy drinking days a few days ago—two bottles of vodka. I haven’t had any since, but I’ve been feeling kind of shaky and anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. We’re watching for signs of alcohol withdrawal, but you’re not showing tremors or high blood pressure, so we don’t think you’re in withdrawal. We’re giving you thiamine and folic acid to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’m trying to cut back and am in a program, but it’s been rough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s really important, especially with your diabetes. We’ve asked social work to talk with you about support after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your blood sugar is coming down—from 700s to the 300s—and your acid levels are improving. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My stomach still hurts, but not as bad as yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed your white blood cell count was high, but your chest X-ray is clear and you don’t have infection signs. It’s likely from the stress on your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we can tell. Your urine culture came back negative, and blood cultures show no growth. The DKA seems to be from not taking your sliding scale insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just didn’t know what dose to take without checking my sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s why we’re going to give you a new glucometer and strips before you go home. Checking your sugar is key to avoiding this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look much better. Your pH is now 7.22, and your creatinine dropped from 1.5 to 1.0—your kidneys are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m feeling less nauseous and actually think I could eat something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll start you on a light meal. Also, we saw some changes on your EKG—T-wave inversions in leads V1-V3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a heart problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but your troponin level is stable and very low. We think it’s ‘demand ischemia’—your heart was under stress from the DKA, not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not a heart attack. But we’ll keep you on your aspirin and statin, and your primary doctor should follow up on this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just got a message from the lab—something about E. coli in my urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ah, yes. That result came in, but it’s likely a contamination. Your urine culture final report showed no growth, and you don’t have symptoms of a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried it meant I needed antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we don’t think so. Your infection markers are down, and you’re improving without antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to move you out of the ICU today. Your insulin drip will be stopped, and you’ll go back to your regular insulin injections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I be going home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We want to make sure you’re eating well and your blood sugar stays stable. We’ll check one more set of labs in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your glucose is 213, which is much better. Your acid levels are nearly normal, and your kidney function has returned to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made excellent progress. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’ll go home with a new glucometer, test strips, and your insulin regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—mirtazapine, venlafaxine, the blood pressure pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications. And please follow up with your primary doctor in two days. They’ll check your heart findings and review your diabetes control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I’ve learned my lesson—no skipping insulin, and I’ll get help with the drinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do for your health. We’re here to support you. Take care, and call if anything comes up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of type 1 diabetes, poorly controlled with prior DKA admissions, alcohol use disorder, depression, and hypertension presented with nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. She was found to be in diabetic ketoacidosis with a blood glucose of 706 and a pH of 6.9, likely due to not taking her sliding scale insulin after losing access to her glucometer, compounded by recent heavy alcohol use. She was treated with IV fluids, an insulin drip, and electrolyte repletion in the ICU. Her condition improved rapidly, with resolution of DKA, normalization of kidney function, and stabilization of vital signs. T-wave inversions on EKG were noted but attributed to demand ischemia from metabolic stress rather than acute coronary syndrome. She was transitioned back to her home insulin regimen, provided with a new glucometer, and discharged home with follow-up instructions. Social work was involved to support ongoing alcohol use counseling.
